webEvidence.snippet: San Telmo and La Boca form the historic heart of Buenos Aires, featuring 19th-century colonial and Italian immigrant architecture, cobblestone streets, and legendary tango roots.
Exploring these two adjacent neighborhoods offers a deep dive into the city's origins as a port town, its waves of immigration, and its enduring artistic identity.

webEvidence.title: Historic Landmarks & Architecture in San Telmo
webEvidence.snippet: San Telmo is the oldest surviving neighborhood in Buenos Aires, characterized by narrow brick walls, colonial casas chorizo (traditional courtyard houses), and uneven cobblestones.

webEvidence.title: Historic Landmarks & Architecture in San Telmo
webEvidence.snippet: DirectionsWebsiteThe historic public square at the center of the neighborhood, famous for hosting the Sunday antiques market (Feria de San Telmo) and surrounded by centuries-old cafes and bars.

webEvidence.title: Historic Landmarks & Architecture in San Telmo
webEvidence.snippet: CallDirectionsWebsiteOpened in 1897, this grand iron-and-timber indoor market on Defensa Street preserves its original structural design while functioning as a bustling hub for food stalls and antiques.

webEvidence.title: Historic Landmarks & Architecture in San Telmo
webEvidence.snippet: A spine of historic continuity lined with colonial-era facades, antique shops, and architectural relics reflecting the early elite who lived here before the 1871 yellow fever epidemic forced them north.

webEvidence.title: Historic Landmarks & Architecture in San Telmo
webEvidence.snippet: CallDirectionsWebsiteA complex of subterranean brick tunnels and restored early-colonial residential ruins that reveal the hidden waterways and changing architecture beneath the neighborhood.

webEvidence.title: Historic Landmarks & Architecture in La Boca
webEvidence.snippet: Just down the riverfront, La Boca grew as a working-class dockworkers' port populated largely by Genoese immigrants who painted their corrugated sheet-metal tenement houses (conventillos) with leftover ship paint.

webEvidence.title: Historic Landmarks & Architecture in La Boca
webEvidence.snippet: CallDirectionsWebsiteA vibrant open-air museum street curated by artist Benito Quinquela Martín, featuring vividly painted tenements, artist workshops, and street tango.

webEvidence.title: Historic Landmarks & Architecture in La Boca
webEvidence.snippet: CallDirectionsWebsiteThe iconic, steep-sided stadium of the Boca Juniors football club, representing the intense cultural and working-class passion of the barrio.

webEvidence.title: Historic Landmarks & Architecture in La Boca
webEvidence.snippet: DirectionsHistoric communal housing units where dozens of immigrant families shared single courtyards and kitchens, showcasing a unique utilitarian industrial architecture.

webEvidence.title: Historic Landmarks & Architecture in La Boca
webEvidence.snippet: The old port zone where European steamships first docked and where the foundational industrial and Afro-Argentine heritage of the area took root.

webEvidence.title: Recommended Walking Itinerary & Tours
webEvidence.snippet: Self-Guided Route: Begin at the edge of San Telmo near Plaza de Mayo, walk down Calle Defensa past colonial facades into Plaza Dorrego, explore the Mercado de San Telmo, and then continue southeast toward La Boca via Avenida Almirante Brown to reach Caminito and the Riachuelo.

webEvidence.title: Recommended Walking Itinerary & Tours
webEvidence.snippet: Guided Options: You can book structured itineraries like the Private La Boca and San Telmo History Walk for expert narrative context on Afro-Argentine history, tango, and local Lunfardo slang, or audio-guided walks via platforms like VoiceMap's San Telmo Tour.
